power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Objectives: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a cyclical hormone-related condition, causing significant mood symptoms in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.
Despite the substantial impact it can have on daily life, little is known about how it shapes reproductive decision-making.
This study explored how people with PMDD experience and reflect on reproductive decisions, and the role of healthcare support in this.
Design: Semi-structured qualitative interviews, informed by a feminist critical realist approach.
Methods: Twenty UK-based adults who had received a diagnosis of, or self-identified as having, PMDD took part.
Semi-structured interviews explored experiences of how, if at all, PMDD had impacted thoughts and decisions around pregnancy or parenthood.
Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, supported by a lived experience advisory group.

Results: Four themes were developed: PMDD as a whole-family experience; intergenerational awareness and responsibility; assessing readiness and capacity for parenthood; and self-advocacy and negotiating an unsupportive system.

Participants not only spoke about how PMDD symptoms shaped their decisionmaking, but also considered relational impact, the potential heritability of PMDD, and the limited healthcare support available.
Support from loved ones, familiarity with their own symptom patterns and establishing strategies for managing PMDD were often described as facilitators of decision-making.
Across themes, findings were interpreted within a "good mother" ideal, helping to explain why reproductive decisions often carried emotional and moral weight.
Conclusions: PMDD can shape reproductive decision-making in complex ways.
Findings demonstrate the need for PMDD-specific support that helps people make informed decisions aligned with their circumstances and needs.

Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a cyclical hormone-related condition, characterised by severe emotional and physical symptoms in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
text.formatted: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a cyclical hormone-related condition, characterised by severe emotional and physical symptoms in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle <ref type="bibr">(American Psychiatric Association, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Common symptoms of PMDD include depression, anxiety and irritability (Halbreich et al., 2003), with significantly heightened risk of suicidal ideation and behaviour (Prasad et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Common symptoms of PMDD include depression, anxiety and irritability <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Halbreich et al., 2003)</ref>, with significantly heightened risk of suicidal ideation and behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Prasad et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The estimated pooled prevalence of PMDD is 3.2% for confirmed diagnosis, rising to around 7% for provisional diagnoses (Reilly et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The estimated pooled prevalence of PMDD is 3.2% for confirmed diagnosis, rising to around 7% for provisional diagnoses <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Reilly et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: PMDD is commonly conceptualised as a disorder of hormonal sensitivity, although its aetiology is likely underpinned by a range of biopsychosocial mechanisms.

The DASH-MC Framework (Dimensional Affective Sensitivity to Hormones across the Menstrual Cycle (Peters et al., 2025)) suggests that symptoms occur as a result of hypersensitivity to fluctuations in oestradiol (E2) and progesterone (P4), with the most severe symptoms arising from surges in allopregnanolone, a metabolite of P4.

text.text: Greater prevalence of early life trauma has also been observed in individuals with PMDD (Kulkarni et al., 2022), and new research also implicates neuroinflammatory pathways (Cheng et al., 2025), indicating that the mechanisms remain complex and not fully understood.

text.text: PMDD is associated with significant social and occupational impairment, contributing an estimated 3,000 days of severe symptoms across the reproductive lifespan (Rapkin & Winer, 2009), impacting relationships (Hodgetts & Kinghorn, 2025), work and education (Brown et al., 2024a) and health-related quality of life (Yang et al., 2008).

text.text: Despite this, research into the experience and impact of PMDD remains limited, with many individuals facing inadequate support (Islas-Preciado et al., 2025; Osborn et al., 2020).

text.text: The cyclical nature of PMDD can lead to identity disruption, losing a sense of self during the symptomatic period, and feeling a need to "overcompensate" once the luteal phase is over (Buys, 2024; Ussher, 2004).

text.text: There is little evidence on how PMDD affects broader life decisions, particularly those relating to reproduction.
This lack of PMDD-specific knowledge may create uncertainty for individuals making decisions about pregnancy and parenthood.
Reproductive decision-making is complex and shaped by emotional, sociocultural, economic and health-related factors (Hashemzadeh et al., 2021).

text.text: Both physical health (Alderotti & Trappolini, 2022; Phillips et al., 2018) and mental health (Krumm & Becker, 2006; Lawley et al., 2022) conditions have been shown to impact people's decisions surrounding pregnancy and parenthood.

text.text: Factors such as medication use, ongoing support needs and risk of worsening mental health have all been reported as reasons for delaying pregnancy or not having children (Lazzari & Beaujouan, 2025).

text.text: For PMDD, given the hormonal nature of the condition, there are other aspects that may be relevant to reproductive decision-making.

Firstly, it is known that PMDD significantly increases risk of perinatal depression (PND), with a Swedish population-cohort study finding that premenstrual disorders were associated with increased risk of both pre-and postnatal depression, with the association slightly stronger for postnatal depression (Yang et al., 2024).

text.text: Despite this, little in-depth work has been done to investigate how and why people with PMDD make these decisions about parenting and what support, if any, they receive from healthcare professionals during this time.
Participants were eligible if they were 18+, lived in the UK and had experience of PMDD.
This included individuals who either self-identified with, or were diagnosed with, PMDD.
This decision was taken due to both the length of time taken to obtain a PMDD diagnosis, and the lack of awareness of PMDD amongst healthcare professionals (Nayak et al., 2025).

text.text: This allowed a greater variety of individuals experiencing PMDD to take part in the study.
Individuals were not required to have experienced pregnancy or thought about reproductive decisions to take part.

Participants were recruited through King's College London Research Recruitment Circular, social media platforms and lived experience networks, allowing for a diverse range of participants to take part.
The concept of information power (Malterud et al., 2016) was followed as an alternative to data saturation.

text.text: Conversations with healthcare providers were also discussed, as well as opinions on availability of support.
The full topic guide for the broader study was developed in collaboration with a lived experience advisory group.
A pilot interview was conducted to assess length and suitability of the topic guide.
Demographic and background information were obtained through an online Qualtrics survey prior to the interview.
The participant information sheet and informed consent form were displayed prior to this on Qualtrics, with full consent required before completing the survey.
The full interview lasted approximately one hour, and participants were given a £20 voucher as a recognition of their time.
Data analysis followed Braun and Clarke's six-step reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006 , 2019).

text.text: Reflexive thematic analysis offers an interpretative approach for exploring patterns of meaning across participants.
This was appropriate for the study aim, which was to understand how people with PMDD made sense of reproductive decision-making.

Reflexive thematic analysis was also a suitable method for the feminist critical realist framing of the study, as analysis considered both participants' accounts, as well as how broader norms and systems shaped the meaning of these experiences.
This means themes were actively developed through engagement with the data, rather than as pre-existing findings.
Inductive analysis was used, promoting a data-driven approach and giving more power to the participants' voices.
Analysis began with repeated reading of the transcripts and note-taking to support familiarisation with the data.
JD then coded the sections of the dataset relevant to reproductive decision-making.

This included semantic codes, such as "concerns about parenting while symptomatic" or "lack of information", as well as latent codes, for example "negotiating the good mother ideal" or "weighing desire against risk".
Codes were reviewed and developed into initial themes, which were discussed with the research team (CJ, CAW, HZ).
A PMDD lived experience advisory group of five individuals also contributed to theme development and refinement.
The group met at three points during the project, including an analysisfocused session after initial coding and theme development.
During this collaborative online session, thematic maps and selected anonymised quotes were shared and discussed.

Reflections from the group shaped several aspects of the analysis, such as highlighting the focus on PMDD as both relational and isolating and reframing intergenerational concerns to better reflect the more positive aspects discussed by some participants.
Following these discussions, the themes were refined and four final themes were developed and defined.
Positionality statement
The first author (JD), who conducted 8 (40%) of the interviews and led the thematic analysis, is a cisgender, heterosexual, White woman.
This positioned her as both an insider and outsider in relation to participants' accounts and therefore this may have impacted how interviews were perceived or interpreted.

The first author discussed reflexivity with a supervisory team (CAW, CJ, HZ), who bring multidisciplinary clinical and academic perspectives, including clinical experience of caring for women with PMDD in the perinatal period, and research expertise in both PMDD and choices around parenthood.
Ethical approval was granted by King's College London Health Faculties (Blue) Research Ethics Subcommittee (reference: HR/DP-24/25-46572).
Participants were provided with information signposting to sources of support, and a distress protocol was also developed in case additional support was required.
Overview of themes Four themes were developed: 1.
PMDD as a whole-family experience 2.
Intergenerational awareness and responsibility 3.
Assessing readiness and capacity for parenthood 4.

Self-advocacy and negotiating an unsupportive system Together, these themes suggest that PMDD shaped reproductive decision-making not only through symptoms themselves, but through how participants imagined the relational, intergenerational and personal consequences of pregnancy and parenthood.

Across the analysis, there was frequent reference towards a "good mother" ideal, which has been used here to reflect gendered expectations of what motherhood "should" look like, situating participants' decisions within societal norms and narratives.

This ideal helped explain why reproductive decisionmaking often carried significant moral weight, with participants considering whether they could be the kind of parent they felt they should be while living with PMDD.
The "good mother" ideal connected the four themes in different ways.
In theme 1, it appeared through concerns about the possible impact of PMDD on partners and family life.
In theme 2, it was reflected in participants' sense of responsibility towards future children.
In theme 3, it shaped how participants assessed their own capacity for parenthood, while in theme 4, it was complicated by the lack of specific information and support.

Theme 1: PMDD as a whole-family experience This theme explores how PMDD shaped reproductive decision-making due to the ways in which participants thought about the possible impact of symptoms on partners, children and family life.
Decisions were often made within a whole-family lens, with considerations as to how PMDD affected those around them.

For example, whether they would be emotionally available, whether they perceived Reproductive Decision-Making in PMDD 11 that they would place too much pressure on their partner, and the possible impact of their symptoms on children.
One participant shared that they were concerned that: "I might just take it out on my child a bit much"
Another described concern that the anger they currently directed towards their partner during symptomatic phases could also affect future children:
Participants who were already parents spoke about their current experiences.

Some spoke about becoming more irritable or overwhelmed during symptomatic phases and described feeling guilty about how this affected their children: "I like snap at the children, speak to them more harshly"

Symptoms of PMDD which made participants want to withdraw from social situations sometimes also had knock-on effects for the child's participation in social activities: "I just don't want to socialise with the other parents… that affects him because he wants to go out with his friends"
This appeared to create a gap between the kind of parent they described wanting to be and the way they sometimes felt when experiencing PMDD symptoms.

These accounts reflected the weight of expectations associated with the "good mother" ideal, particularly the idea that mothers should be consistently emotionally available, patient and able to protect children from distress: "I just get very hopeless...that then feeds into how you feel about family life and about your parenting"
Participants who were not parents spoke about similar worries they associated with parenting and how this contributed to reproductive decision-making:
However, family was also a crucial support system for many participants.

Supportive partners, and effective communication, reconnection and repair after symptomatic periods were described to be important, and some participants discussed how this made the idea of parenthood feel possible.

Being able to survive challenging experiences as a family was seen to strengthen relationships and support for one another, and this was reflected in how participants spoke about hope in reproductive decisionmaking: "Connection is one of the things that helps me" "There would also be somebody else taking care of the child...

I think it's manageable" Therefore, while participants spoke about the difficulties in parenting with PMDD, and how this impacted reproductive decisions, it was often a matter of weighing up difficulties against a system of whole-family support.
A tension within this theme was that PMDD was often described relationally but also experienced as isolating.

Participants recognised that PMDD affected those around them, but also described withdrawing from others, feeling alone with their symptoms, or struggling to explain what they were experiencing: "It impacts my relationships…I just feel like…everybody's out to kind of get me…I broke up with my boyfriend in that kind of period but we're back together because a week later I was like, I didn't need to do that"
This could mean that at times, it was harder to access support from family, and it was in these moments of isolation where complex and emotional reproductive decisions felt much more challenging.
Theme 2: Intergenerational awareness and responsibility
This theme focuses on how reproductive decision-making was viewed in relation to own childhood experiences, as well as experiences for future potential children.

Considering their own childhood, some participants reflected that they thought their own mothers experienced PMDD, and spoke about the impact this had on their childhood, seeing their mother withdraw for periods of time or having their other parent "shield" them from her during symptomatic periods.
Some participants were anxious of repeating patterns; sharing that: "I was like a bit scared of my mum...
I just wouldn't have seen her for like days...
I don't want my children to have that experience"
However, others also discussed their childhood experiences as reassuring.

Participants who felt their mother had experienced symptoms of PMDD spoke about how they had a childhood filled with love and care, and participants were confident they would be able to provide a similar nurturing environment if they chose to have a child: "My mum has had it and she managed to raise me...not really that much of a worry"
Looking toward the future, some participants spoke about feeling a sense of moral responsibility to avoid passing PMDD on to future children.
They also mentioned how difficult they found experiencing symptoms of PMDD, and with uncertainty as to the genetic nature of the condition, did not want to risk passing PMDD onto a future child.
This was a significant worry for some and was sometimes the catalyst for reproductive decisions: "Passing on what I described as debilitating...genes...
I did not wish to do that" "If I have...a female child, then they might get PMDD, and that makes it quite sad"
However, positives of such awareness were also shared.
Some participants felt that awareness of PMDD could be protective.
Knowing about PMDD, having a name for it and understanding symptoms could make it possible to respond differently to a future child's needs.
Participants discussed hope for the future, with more research hopefully bringing better treatment or support, making the possibility of their child experiencing PMDD less worrisome:
This theme links to the "good mother" ideal through expectations of maternal protection and responsibility.
Participants' concerns about inheritance or repeating difficult family patterns demonstrated a sense of responsibility towards a future child.
However, participants did not only imagine protection through avoiding parenthood.
For some, their own awareness of PMDD offered the possibility of creating a different family environment or responding differently to symptoms.
Theme 3: Assessing readiness and capacity for parenthood This theme explores how participants assessed whether, when and how parenthood might feel possible while living with PMDD.
PMDD did not lead to one clear reproductive pathway.
Instead, it shaped how participants weighed up risk, desire, uncertainty, loss and hope when imagining their future.
For some, it was a major factor in deciding not to have children, or in delaying parenthood.
"I decided not to have children.

That was a sobering decision…a lot of my aggression stemmed from this particular condition…it has nothing to do with the maternal instinct" For others, it was one consideration among many: "[PMDD] definitely didn't put me off...we just waited a little longer" While for some participants, regardless of whether they wanted children or not, it didn't feel like a factor in the decision: "I'm not sure I can see a way that PMDD has influenced my thinking around that" "I'm not sure that [PMDD] would influence the process of having children"
Participants discussed how the intensity of symptoms, as well as the cross-cycle symptom variation, might impact their capacity to cope with the demands of parenting.

Participants expressed that they would often revisit reproductive decisions and would assess how stable they currently felt, as well as how they envisaged future treatment and greater awareness shaping their experiences: "I just feel like I'll be able to grow by then and I'll be able to manage a way more…I'm gonna be hopefully way more equipped"
Medication and hormonal treatment also shaped how participants thought about reproductive decisionmaking.

For some, symptom management of PMDD relied largely on hormonal contraception, with the prospect of pausing this for a potential pregnancy feeling like an impossibility: "I am like at a period in my life where I feel like I'm scared to not be on the pill" Many participants experienced Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS, previously PCOS) as a co-occurring condition, which is known to have implications for fertility, thus contributing to decision-making.
For some of these participants, questions about whether, when and how to have children were not only shaped by PMDD, but also by concerns about fertility.
This could create an additional sense of pressure, as participants felt they may need to make decisions about parenthood before feeling emotionally ready:
Participants also raised concerns about the postpartum period, with worries as to how their mental health would be impacted by such a significant hormonal transition.
Some participants were aware of the increased risk of postpartum depression in PMDD: "PMDD like really has just made me very fearful of having children...made me decide not to have children...

I worry that I would be more predisposed to having some form of postnatal condition"; while others feared significant PMDD symptom exacerbation following childbirth: "I don't know if pregnancy can make it worse or not...like after pregnancy it can get like 100 times worse"
These concerns did not always lead participants away from parenthood, but they did shape how they imagined the timing and conditions under which parenthood might be possible.

On the other hand, a few of the participants who were mothers described their experiences of pregnancy as providing peace and stability, viewing pregnancy and the immediate postpartum period as a positive period with no regular menstrual cycle to produce PMDD symptoms: "My mood was really stable and I felt kind of really calm throughout the pregnancies"
Having to consider one's own readiness and capacity for parenthood can be an emotional subject, with participants discussing feelings of sadness and grief in relation to decision-making.
For some, decisions about delaying or not pursuing parenthood were framed through concern for a future child's wellbeing: "I still feel it would have been so unfair to the child, first of all.
And yeah, this was a dilemma that I weighed on for years.
This wasn't some sudden decision…Why have a child to satisfy myself?"
A sense of hope was also noticeable, with participants feeling that with more time to learn about PMDD and how to best manage it, their readiness or capacity for parenthood would change.
"In trying to manage it and control it right now, when I'm younger, in the hope that when I actually do…think about pregnancy and having children, hopefully it will be better managed"
Overall, the "good mother" ideal was particularly visible in this theme.
Participants evaluated whether they felt able to meet a child's needs while living with PMDD.
For some, delaying parenthood or deciding not to have children was framed by participants not as a lack of desire, but as an attempt to make a responsible decision in relation to a future child.
"I think I would not be a good enough mother, having to deal with these issues"
Theme 4: Self-advocacy and negotiating an unsupportive system This theme focuses on the role of healthcare, information and support in reproductive decision-making.
Participants discussed the difficulty of making reproductive decisions without adequate PMDD-specific guidance.

Participants sought information about symptom changes in pregnancy and the postpartum period, whether PMDD introduced specific susceptibility to any perinatal conditions, and medication usage during the perinatal period: "If I start medication, and like if I plan to, I don't know, get pregnant next year or the year after like would that be an issue or if you're like breastfeeding?"
Most participants were unsure, but doubtful, about the existence of any specific guidance on PMDD in the perinatal period: "There's not a leaflet about PMDD let alone family planning about it"

Participants often reported that the only information they had seen was anecdotal, in community groups or online forums: "I have also read sort of anecdotally about people whose PMDD has become worse since they have had children"
Some participants had actively sought advice or guidance from a healthcare professional.
Participants often described healthcare professionals as lacking knowledge about PMDD, dismissing concerns or offering advice that felt overly simplistic and unprofessional.

For example, discussing pregnancy as a route to symptom relief, without attention given to postpartum mental health or the practical realities of caring for a child: "The gynaecologist...was almost encouraging me to have a child because she was saying your symptoms improved during pregnancy...but what about afterwards?"
These encounters left some participants feeling unsupported, or as though they had to understand the mechanisms of PMDD for themselves.
Other participants discussed negative experiences with healthcare professionals when seeking information about more permanent PMDD treatment options, such as a hysterectomy.

They were made to feel this was not an appropriate treatment, as they were yet to have a child: "The most discussion I've had is with a gynaecologist and saying…can I get a hysterectomy like is that possible?
And they said to me well, you haven't had children yet"
In order to obtain appropriate care or onward referral, participants had to endure constant self-advocacy, educating healthcare professionals and negotiating between services.

Most participants did not feel that they had access to informative healthcare support, however one participant did describe an appointment with a specialist who provided some PMDD-specific information relevant to the perinatal period.
Reproductive decision-making was therefore not only shaped by PMDD symptoms, but also by the difficulty of navigating systems that did not understand the relevance of PMDD to these conversations.

When it came to what more they wanted from healthcare professionals, participants were clear: they wanted information and time to discuss their concerns with knowledgeable professionals: "There needs to be a lot of information to support women making this decision because it is a huge deal…so I think, you know, whoever it may be, GP, gynaecologist, psychiatrist, you know, should be giving the pros and cons" Without this, they were left to make uncertain decisions.

Participants highlighted research as a beneficial tool for informing healthcare professionals' knowledge: "Well, it would be helpful to start with some research in the area to gather the thoughts of women like myself"
This theme extends the "good mother" ideal into the healthcare context.
Participants described uncertainty around pregnancy, postpartum mental health and family life, alongside limited PMDD-specific guidance from healthcare professionals.
This placed responsibility heavily on the individual, as participants were often left to search for information, educate professionals and advocate for their own care.

Some participants discussed healthcare encounters that centred future fertility or motherhood, for example questioning treatment preferences because a participant had not yet had children, which is reflective of the "good mother" ideal.
This study explored how people with PMDD experience reproductive decision-making.

Four themes were constructed: PMDD as a whole-family experience; intergenerational awareness and responsibility; assessing readiness and capacity for parenthood; and self-advocacy and negotiating an unsupportive system.
The findings suggest that while PMDD can shape reproductive decisions in complex ways, it does not lead towards one single outcome.

Across interviews, decision-making was shaped not only by symptoms themselves, but by relational impact, feelings of responsibility towards future children, assessments of own parenting capacity and experiences of limited healthcare support.
The moral weight of reproductive decision-making expressed by participants in this study can be understood in relation to good mother ideology and the wider concept of intensive mothering.

Good mother ideology positions mothers as responsible for prioritising children's needs and child-rearing above Reproductive Decision-Making in PMDD 20 all else (Williamson et al., 2023), with intensive mothering further emphasising self-sacrifice, emotional availability and responsibility for children's wellbeing (Hays, 1996).

text.text: While these concepts have been widely used to understand experiences of motherhood, they have received limited attention in relation to PMDD.
The present study therefore extends this literature by showing how expectations of emotionally available, protective and child-focused motherhood may shape decision-making while living with PMDD.

This was evident in concerns about the impact of symptoms on children and partners, fears about passing PMDD on and assessments of whether participants felt stable or prepared enough to parent in the way they wanted.
These findings also have implications for how voluntary childlessness is understood in the context of PMDD.
Motherhood is often assumed as expected, natural or desirable (Ussher, 2005), however in this study, some participants were choosing not to have children or to delay parenthood.

text.text: This suggests that some healthcare professionals may be prioritising potential future motherhood over patient preferences, with an assumption that fertility preservation should take precedence.
Another key finding of this study is that reproductive decision-making in PMDD was often relational rather than purely individual.
Participants did not only consider whether they personally wanted children, but also how PMDD in this context may impact partners and other family members.
For example, some expressed concern that during their luteal phase, they would be placing too much parenting burden on their partners.

However, some participants also spoke about how important support from their partner or wider family was, and how this made the potential of parenthood feel possible, as they would not be managing alone.
In previous work, supportive partners, open communication and a team-based approach to child-rearing helped some mothers navigate the pressures of good mother ideology (Williamson et al., 2023).

text.text: Similarly, here, reproductive decision-making was partially shaped by the presence or absence of relational support.

Given this, support around PMDD and reproductive decision-making may therefore need to include discussion of partners and wider family support, rather than focusing only on individual symptom management.
The interviews involved both parents and non-parents, allowing the analysis to explore current or past decision-making experiences alongside imagined futures.

The involvement of a lived experience advisory group also supported reflexive engagement with the developing analysis, particularly around language, sensitivity and avoiding an overly deterministic account of PMDD and parenthood.
However, the findings should be interpreted in relation to the study sample and context.
Participants were predominantly highly educated, and all described their gender identity as female.
The analysis may therefore not fully explore how PMDD and reproductive decision-making is experienced by different sociocultural contexts.
In addition, the use of the "good mother" ideal as an interpretative lens largely reflects a Western view of motherhood and may not be applicable across different cultures.

Recommendations for research and clinical practice Future research should explore healthcare professionals' knowledge and experiences of supporting people with PMDD around the preconception and perinatal periods.
This would help identify training needs and opportunities for clinical guidance.

Further work should also include more diverse participant groups, including people from a wider range of socioeconomic backgrounds, people living in non-Western contexts, and trans and non-binary people who experience PMDD.
Finally, given the relational nature of the findings, research with partners and family members may also help explore how PMDD is understood and supported within family systems.
These findings have several implications for clinical practice.
Importantly, PMDD should be recognised as relevant to preconception care, the perinatal period and reproductive decision-making.
People with PMDD need non-judgemental support which acknowledges one's own reproductive autonomy.
This should include opportunities to discuss symptom management, medication, pregnancy, postpartum mental health, parenting concerns and family support.
Accessible PMDD-specific patient information or decision aids may also help to reduce uncertainty and support more informed decision-making.
In conclusion, the current study found that PMDD can shape reproductive decision-making in complex and varied ways.
Participants' decisions were not only influenced by symptoms, but by concerns about family life, parenting capacity and the availability of support.
The findings demonstrate the need for PMDD-specific, non-judgemental support, so that people with PMDD can make informed decisions that align with their own values and circumstances.
